vignette:
He is a 22-year-old South Eastern Asian man who comes across as careful and contained, the sort of person who has learned to keep his voice steady even when he is describing something terrible. Before the war, he is a student with ordinary plans: classes, exams, friendships, and the vague, hopeful sense that adulthood will open in front of him in a manageable way. When the conflict worsens, he volunteers as a relief worker, telling himself that he can be useful, that he can carry water, sort supplies, translate, do something practical while other people around him are panicking. At first, the work gives shape to his days. He feels needed. He also feels a growing tension in his chest that he ignores because there is no time to notice it.

The traumatic experiences build gradually, then all at once. He speaks of the war zone in fragments: roads blocked by shelling, the smell of smoke and dust, children waiting in lines for food, mothers asking for medicine that has run out. He learns to move quickly and not look too long at what is broken. One day, while distributing aid, there is an explosion nearby. He does not describe it dramatically; he says only that the world becomes white, then loud, then strangely quiet. Afterward he cannot remember the sequence of certain moments. He knows there are injured people on the ground and that he is helping drag one man behind a wall, his hands slick with someone else's blood. Later he learns that someone he had spoken to earlier is dead. The fact settles in him like a stone. He keeps working, partly because others are still there, partly because stopping feels impossible, and partly because he does not yet understand that his body has already started to memorize the danger.

When he returns home, he expects relief. Instead, ordinary life feels unreal and thin. He is back in school, sitting in lecture halls, but he often cannot follow what is being said. His mind drifts to checkpoints, sirens, the sound of rubble falling. He sits near exits and scans the room without meaning to. He notices every sudden noise: a dropped backpack, a motorbike backfiring in the street, a door slamming shut. His shoulders tighten before he even understands why. He sleeps lightly and wakes quickly, sometimes convinced he has heard the whine of aircraft or the crack of an explosion. On some nights he dreams he is back in the aid station, trying to count boxes while wounded people call for help in voices he cannot reach. He wakes with his heart racing and spends long minutes staring at the ceiling, trying to convince himself of the date, the room, the city he is in now.

He becomes increasingly avoidant. He stops watching the news, then stops checking social media because images of rubble or injured children send a jolt through him that can last for hours. He does not talk about his work in the war zone unless he has to, and even then he keeps it vague, as if details might make the memories more real. When classmates ask how he managed to do such work, he changes the subject. He finds himself avoiding crowded places because he dislikes being trapped. He takes longer routes home so he does not pass construction sites where loud bangs might startle him. He notices that he sits with his back to walls and prefers windows closed, curtains drawn, the apartment quiet. His friends say he is distant. He knows he is, but it feels less like distance than enclosure, as if something inside him has shut a door.

He is also more irritable than he used to be. Small frustrations-an unanswered message, a class schedule change, someone speaking too loudly-can make him feel hot with anger that arrives before he can think. He then feels ashamed of that anger and tries to contain it, which leaves him exhausted. There are moments when guilt breaks through with unusual force. He thinks about the people who were waiting for aid, the ones he could not help enough, the one he saw die, and he wonders why he came back when others did not. At times he questions whether he should have done more, stayed longer, been braver. These thoughts do not come in orderly sentences; they come as sudden waves that interrupt him while he is reading, eating, or walking across campus.

Since returning, he has become more self-conscious about his own body. He notices his heartbeat, his breathing, the tension in his jaw. He seems to live in a state of watchfulness, as though his mind has never fully left the war zone and is still waiting for the next blast. He tries to keep up with his studies, but concentration takes effort, and he often rereads the same page without absorbing it. He is not without moments of warmth-he still answers his family's calls, still goes to class, still makes careful plans-but these are threaded through with a constant sense of danger that he cannot switch off. His life now is organized around not being surprised, not being overwhelmed, not letting the memory of that place catch him unprepared.
